prompt: What decides which view goes in front of a room?
hint: Lesson 1: a diagram answers a question.

choices.text: The view the architect spent most time on
choices.why: That is the pride the lesson warns about: the detailed picture is usually the wrong one for a high room.

choices.text: What the people in the room decide
choices.why: Right: the question is theirs, so the view has to be the one that answers it.

choices.text: The most recent view in the model, whatever its level
choices.why: Recency says nothing about whether it answers the room's question.

choices.text: A fixed company standard of one slide per container
choices.why: No such rule fits three rooms that decide different things.

prompt: Which view did Tainá show the directors on Monday?
hint: Money, dates, the risk at São João.

choices.text: The container diagram with every protocol
choices.why: Containers are for people who build or run the system; the directors never saw one.

choices.text: The state table of the boarding app
choices.why: That went to the engineers on Thursday.

choices.text: The system context, with the new link marked
choices.why: Right: the highest view, with the one thing the decision was about marked on it.

choices.text: A component diagram of the boarding sync service
choices.why: Components are for the team that owns one container.

prompt: A meeting has a director and three engineers. Where does the lesson say to start?

choices.text: At the highest level anybody there needs
choices.why: Right: the engineers follow the context, and the director would not follow the containers.

choices.text: At the container level, since the engineers are the majority
choices.why: The director would be lost from the first slide, and the decision is theirs.

choices.text: With two separate decks shown one after the other
choices.why: Twice the time, and each half of the room waits through the other's deck.

choices.text: At the code level, to show that the work is real
choices.why: Nobody in a mixed room needs code to take an architectural decision.

prompt: Match each of the course's frameworks to how it helps choose a view for an audience.

pairs.right: zoom levels, from context for anybody to components for one team
rows, each an audience with its own vocabulary
viewpoints designed for a stakeholder's concern

right_distractors: a fixed slide template for every meeting

prompt: The directors' old deck showed the station back office, already retired. What does the lesson say that wrong box cost?

choices.text: Only the time to fix the slide
choices.why: The fix is quick; the trust lost with it is not.

choices.text: The engineers' trust in the rest of the slides
choices.why: Right: everybody who spotted one wrong box doubted the others.

choices.text: A wrong decision about the back office
choices.why: Nothing was decided on that slide; the damage was to belief.

choices.text: A delay to the São João release
choices.why: The lesson describes no delay.

prompt: With every slide a view exported from one model, what may the three decks still differ in?
hint: One model does not mean one look.

choices.text: Which system owns the bookings
choices.why: That is a fact, and the decks may not disagree about facts.

choices.text: The order, the words and what each view includes
choices.why: Right: everything that is not a fact of the model may change per room.

choices.text: Whether the back office still exists
choices.why: Another fact: the model says it once for every deck.

choices.text: The names of the elements, translated for each audience
choices.why: Renaming per deck is exactly how decks start to disagree.

prompt: A team has no tool that generates views from a model. What does the lesson keep of the rule?

choices.text: Nothing: without generation every deck is drawn fresh
choices.why: The lesson keeps a weaker form of the rule.

choices.text: One owned, dated place to copy diagrams from
choices.why: Right: the source stays single even when the export is manual.

choices.text: Ask the presenter to redraw the diagrams before each meeting
choices.why: Redrawing is how three different drawings of one system appear.

choices.text: Send the model file instead of slides
choices.why: A model file is not a presentation, and the rooms still need views.

prompt: Why build a diagram up in steps instead of showing it whole?

choices.text: Shown whole, each person reads it in a different order while the presenter talks
choices.why: Right: built up, everybody looks at what the next sentence needs.

choices.text: Because projectors draw large diagrams slowly
choices.why: It is about attention, not hardware.

choices.text: To make the presentation last longer
choices.why: The steps take seconds; they replace confusion, not time.

choices.text: Because the notation of C4 requires it
choices.why: C4 says nothing about how a diagram is revealed.

prompt: Put the three steps in which Tainá built up the context diagram for the directors in order.
hint: The line the review is about comes last.
items: the passenger and the ticketing system
the 26 stations and their link, in amber
trap: The amber line comes last, so that when it appears everybody already knows what it connects.

prompt: Which element should a walk through a diagram begin at, in a room of directors?

choices.text: The booking database
choices.why: Nobody in a non-technical room can stand there.

choices.text: The element with the most connections on the diagram
choices.why: The busiest box is not the most familiar one.

choices.text: The passenger, following what a passenger does
choices.why: Right: begin at a person the audience recognises and follow them.

choices.text: Whichever box is at the top left of the slide
choices.why: Layout position is not a reason; the reader's footing is.

prompt: Instead of saying "as you can see here", ___ the element you point at, for the people on a call who cannot see your hand.
hint: Somebody on a phone has only the words.

prompt: What is the most useful rule for drawing a before-and-after pair?
hint: The way the eye compares two photos.

choices.text: Draw the after picture larger, so the change is noticed first
choices.why: Size changes make the eye compare sizes, not content.

choices.text: Keep every element in the same place in both pictures
choices.why: Right: then the eye finds the difference on its own.

choices.text: Use a different layout tool for each of the two pictures
choices.why: Two tools would move the elements, which is the problem.

choices.text: Show only the after picture
choices.why: Then nobody sees what changed.

prompt: Why does the lesson mark a change with a word or shape as well as a colour?

choices.text: Colour alone fails for people who do not tell the colours apart, on washed-out projectors and on grey printouts
choices.why: Right: about one man in twelve does not tell red from green, and the word survives every medium.

choices.text: Because the slide template has no colours
choices.why: Colour is used; it is just not used alone.

choices.text: Because words are easier to export from a model
choices.why: Export has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: To make the slide look busier
choices.why: The marks are there to be read, not to fill space.

prompt: Why draw a retired element dashed and labelled retired, instead of leaving it out?

choices.text: So nobody wonders whether it was forgotten
choices.why: Right: an element that simply vanishes looks like an omission.

choices.text: Because the model cannot delete elements
choices.why: Models can delete them; the point is what the reader sees.

choices.text: To keep the slide the same width
choices.why: Width is not the reason.

choices.text: Because retired elements still take part in the purchase flow
choices.why: A retired element takes part in nothing.

prompt: The digital boarding programme takes a year. What did the product team actually want to see?
hint: Lesson 8's word for the states in between.

choices.text: Only the target architecture
choices.why: The target was not their question; the year in between was.

choices.text: The next transition, with its date
choices.why: Right: what a station looks like in May, halfway through, is what people will live in.

choices.text: The full list of tickets in the project tracker
choices.why: That is work, not architecture.

choices.text: The baseline, since nothing changes until the end
choices.why: Things change at every transition, not only at the end.

prompt: What did the directors see from the review's fourteen risks?

choices.text: All fourteen, ranked by severity
choices.why: The ranked list was in the report; the directors saw what it added up to.

choices.text: The theme, and what depends on it
choices.why: Right: one theme is a decision a director can take; fourteen risks are a list.

choices.text: Only the risks with a high likelihood of happening
choices.why: Filtering by likelihood hides the pattern that made the theme.

choices.text: None of them: risks are for engineers
choices.why: The risk was the whole reason for the meeting.

prompt: Why put the source of each number on the slide, under the number?

choices.text: It answers the first question before it is asked, and shows the number was measured
choices.why: Right: 2,000 purchases a minute with QS-01 and a load test beside it is evidence.

choices.text: Because the law requires sources on business slides
choices.why: No law is involved.

choices.text: So the slide can be printed without the presenter
choices.why: The source helps, but the reason is credibility in the room.

choices.text: To fill the empty space under the chart
choices.why: It is small and there for a reason, not to fill space.

prompt: How did Tainá put the one-link-per-station risk to the directors?

choices.text: As the number of network devices installed at each station
choices.why: That is the engineer's unit.

choices.text: As forty people in a queue who cannot buy a ticket
choices.why: Right: the same risk, in the unit the reader counts.

choices.text: As a percentage of uptime for the station routers
choices.why: Uptime percentages are still the engineer's unit.

choices.text: By showing the network diagram of a station
choices.why: A lower view, for a room that decides higher.

prompt: How many parts does the lesson say each slide with a diagram carries?
Which of these does the lesson ask of a diagram on a slide? Choose all that apply.
hint: The back row, the call, the phone.

choices.text: a title that states the claim in a full sentence
choices.why: Yes: read alone, the title makes the point.

choices.text: a footer with the model's version, date and owner
choices.why: Yes: a slide forwarded in six months says how old it is.

choices.text: about seven to nine elements
choices.why: Yes: more than that is a document page, not a slide.

choices.text: the protocol on every line
choices.why: Lines carry short verbs; the protocol belongs in the document.

prompt: Match each part of the pack Tainá sent after a meeting to the lesson that produced it.
hint: None of it was new work.

pairs.left: the views shown, with version and date
the findings with owners and dates

prompt: A month after the meeting, Bento reads the pack to learn why the stations have two links. Which part answers him best?

choices.text: The views shown, since the second link is drawn on them
choices.why: The views show the link; they do not say why it was chosen.

choices.text: The open questions, since they list what is still unclear
choices.why: They say what is unknown, not what was decided.

choices.text: The paragraph on the decision, with the records it links to
choices.why: Right: the decision, who took it and when, and the records hold the reasons.

choices.text: The findings in the tracker, since each one has an owner and a date
choices.why: Findings say what was at risk and who acted, not why the answer was a second link.
